description: We're a team of students from the German University In Cairo who love building apps and websites, and we're excited to take on our first NASA Space Apps Challenge! We're planning to work on Creating Health Monitoring Software For Astronauts on Space Missions, turning real NASA data into an interactive tool people can actually use.
summary: NABD ("pulse" in Arabic) is a daily health check-in for astronauts on missions too far from Earth to call a doctor, built for the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". In 4 minutes, a phone reads the astronaut's face, voice and reaction time, compares them with her own normal, and gives four readiness scores with one concrete step for today. It adds a body map grounded in NASA's human spaceflight risks, an AI doctor that works with the ship's medical kit and flags emergencies even offline, private women's health tracking, and family contact. Mission Control and the flight surgeon each see only what their role needs. It matters because small changes in sleep, mood and health build up quietly, and astronauts often don't report them; NABD catches them early. It is also useful anywhere help is far away.

TRY IT: https://nabd-nasa-space-apps.vercel.app (best on a phone; on a laptop use Chrome → Inspect → device mode for the crew app. Mission Control and the flight surgeon are designed for laptops.)

Crew: tap Sara Haddad, PIN 1404 (also Adam 2201, Mei 3302, Lucas 4403). Mission Control: any email and password. Flight surgeon: after Mission Control, go to /surgeon. Family: /send. Code: https://github.com/malakanwarr/Nabd-NASA-Space-Apps

NABD (نبض, "pulse" in Arabic) is a daily health check-in for astronauts who are too far from Earth to call a doctor. Team MoonWalkerz · NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026 · Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.

THE PROBLEM

On a Mars mission a message to Earth takes up to 20 minutes each way. The flight surgeon cannot see the crew every day, and NASA notes that astronauts can be reluctant to report when they are struggling. Small changes in sleep, mood, bone and heart build up quietly until they become a problem.

WHAT EXACTLY DOES IT DO?

NABD is one web app (installable on a phone, works offline) with four views, each built for one person's job:

- Crew member: a 4-minute morning check-in that reads her face (blink rate, eyelid openness, smiles), her voice (loudness, pitch range, pauses, pace) and her reactions (the Pollen catch game, based on NASA's vigilance test), plus six sleep questions. NABD compares every number with her own normal and returns four separate scores, never one diagnosis: cognitive readiness, physical readiness, sleep recovery and emotional wellbeing. Each is shown as Stable, Watch or Act, with the reason, a 7-day trend and one next step.

- Body map: a clickable astronaut with eight body systems (bones and muscles, mind and sleep, kidneys, heart, eyes, immune system, radiation, cycle). Each shows what it does, why space affects it and its NASA hazard, her own numbers and trend, what to do today, and when to get help.

- Act on it: "Adjust my workout" builds a plan from her muscle strength, energy and cycle, and a muscle "twin" does every move with her. Guided measurements (for example blood sugar) explain how to measure in space and what the result means.

- AI doctor that works without Earth: answers with her own data and the ship's medical kit, cites NASA research, never diagnoses, and shows an emergency banner with "Call the crew medical officer" for danger signs, checked before the AI is even called. She decides which answers go to her flight surgeon.

- No male default: private cycle tracking or period suppression that adjusts what counts as normal for each phase. Only she sees it.

- Habitat garden: sleep, water, exercise, vitamin D and mood become plants that grow or droop.

- Family: relatives hold one button to send a hug that makes her phone buzz, and see only her heartbeat and a simple mood. She has a "window home" with her family's avatars and messages.

- Mission Control (laptop): every crew member's status, readiness, last check-in and alerts, with filters and "add crew member". It never sees cycle data, face or voice details, or AI doctor chats.

- Flight surgeon (laptop): vitals, allergies and the AI doctor's notes with their send and arrival times, the cycle summary only with consent, and replies that show "reaches the ship in about 18 minutes".

HOW DOES IT WORK?

- On the phone, offline: Google MediaPipe Face Landmarker runs in the browser and turns about 10 frames a second into three numbers; the voice check (Meyda and pitchy) keeps four numbers from the first word to the last. Video and audio never leave the phone.

- Her own baseline: each score drops by how far each signal moves in the "tired" direction, weighted, with missing signals dropped and the rest reweighted. It reproduces all six days of our sample astronaut's history exactly (84, 82, 83, 74, 70, 66).

- AI doctor: Google Gemini with a summary of her data and a knowledge base built from NASA Human Research Program material; red flags are checked on the server first; safe fallback if the AI is unavailable.

- One React app and one Node/Express server with MongoDB, deployed on Vercel. The signed-in role (crew, Mission Control, flight surgeon, family) decides every page and every API answer.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

- The astronaut notices slow changes she might not report, and gets a concrete step for today.

- Mission Control sees who needs attention at a glance; the flight surgeon gets useful notes despite the delay.

- Privacy by design: each role sees only what it should.

- Beyond Mars: anyone far from a doctor (polar stations, ships, remote communities) needs only a phone.

HOW WE TESTED IT

- Energy score matches all six sample days of our fictional astronaut.

- Fatigue experiment: we tested NABD on one team member, on Friday afternoon (her baseline) and again on Saturday morning after a 13-hour hackathon day and about 6 hours of sleep. Against her own normal, NABD labelled the second check-in "tired" (72 vs. 84): 6 of 8 signals moved in the tired direction, led by smiling (-80%) and voice pitch range (-62%).

- AI doctor safety tests: 10 scripted questions, each run twice; 10 of 10 passed both runs. Chest pain and low oxygen always gave the emergency answer first; it refused amoxicillin (penicillin allergy) and doses above the label; it linked symptoms to her own data and cited NASA correctly. The emergency word check, which works without the AI, was 20 of 20 correct with no false alarms. Offline mode gave 3 of 3 safe answers in 0.2 seconds.

- Face, voice and game check-in tested on iPhone over HTTPS.

Limits: a prototype, not a medical device; thresholds need clinical testing. Sara's history is fictional sample data, with vitals and sleep standing in for the wearables crews already wear; the check-in, game, AI doctor and hugs are live. Sign-in is simulated. The fatigue test is one person, one night and a different time of day: a first signal, not proof.

WHAT DO WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE?

Test with analog crews (HERA, Antarctic stations), run the AI doctor on the spacecraft with a local model, connect real wearables, and review every threshold with flight surgeons.

INTENDED IMPACT

Catch health changes days before they become a problem, when no doctor is in reach, and give the crew, Mission Control and the flight surgeon the right picture without overloading or exposing anyone. The same phone-only check-in can serve polar stations, ships and remote communities on Earth.

HOW IS IT CREATIVE?

- No wearables or lab needed: a 4-minute check-in on any phone reads fatigue from face, voice and a reaction game.

- Compared with HER normal, not a population average, and never one diagnosis: four scores, each with a reason and one step.

- An AI doctor designed for 20-minute delays: it uses only the ship's kit, cites NASA, and catches emergencies with a keyword check before the AI and even offline.

- No male default: the cycle adjusts what counts as normal, privately.

- Human touches that matter on long missions: a garden that grows with healthy habits, and family hugs that make her phone buzz.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Privacy: video and audio never leave the phone, and each role sees only what it should (Mission Control never sees cycle, face/voice details or AI chats; the surgeon sees the cycle only with consent).

- Safety: no diagnosis, label doses only, allergy checks, emergency escalation to the crew medical officer, and a tested offline fallback.

- Communication delay and no internet: works offline; surgeon replies show their arrival time.

- Under-reporting: a short, friendly daily routine instead of asking astronauts to report problems.

- Women's health and the fact that crews differ: personal baselines and cycle-aware norms.

- Honesty: we label sample data, simulated sign-in and the limits of our small tests.

TOOLS

React, Vite, React Router, vite-plugin-pwa, Recharts · Google MediaPipe Face Landmarker, Web Audio API, Meyda, pitchy · Node.js, Express, MongoDB Atlas, Mongoose, Vercel · Google Gemini API · JavaScript, HTML, CSS · Hardware: any phone with a camera and microphone, and a laptop. AI assistance: Claude and Claude Code (planning, design, code), Gemini (AI doctor), Manus (documents); all ideas and decisions are the team's.
